units.text: In this video, you'll follow a Lambda event and choose a compatible way to package the function. A photo upload can start thumbnailing without a server waiting for it. Follow the source S three bucket, the object-created event and the Lambda handler. The destination S three bucket holds the thumbnail after that execution environment disappears.

The runtime can be reused, but the thumbnail does not depend on it. A W S operates the compute platform. The application still needs permission to write the result and a duplicate-handling rule, for example a stable output key.

When EventBridge supplies an event, Lambda initializes a compatible environment as needed and invokes the handler. A later invocation may reuse that environment. Store durable output in Dynamo D B or S three so a replacement does not erase the application's state.

The responsibility split matters. A W S runs and scales the platform. You own the code, dependencies, permissions, input validation, idempotency and whether downstream systems can handle the resulting traffic.

Match the package to the runtime contract. A zip can use a supported managed runtime. A Lambda container image is stored in E C R and must use a compatible Linux architecture and implement the Lambda Runtime A P I, typically through a runtime interface client.

A generic server container is not automatically a Lambda image. If the goal is to keep an ordinary application container running as a service, consider E C S with capacity such as Fargate instead. Whichever packaging route you take, patch the dependencies you own.

In this video, you'll size Lambda's memory and storage, check payload limits, and choose the right concurrency control. Memory, temporary disk and execution time solve different problems. An Event Function can be configured from 128 to 10,240 megabytes of memory, with more C P U as memory goes up. At 1,769 megabytes, the allocation is equivalent to one virtual C P U. Benchmark duration and cost rather than guessing.

The slash tmp setting controls separate ephemeral storage, from 512 to 10,240 megabytes. Use it for intermediate files, not durable state. After the November update, an on-demand Event Function can run for up to 30 minutes; an upstream caller or integration may stop waiting much sooner.

Separate deployment size from invocation size. A direct zip upload is limited to 50 megabytes compressed; uncompressed code plus layers is capped at 250 megabytes. A compatible container image can be up to 10 gigabytes uncompressed. None of those numbers is the size of an event you can invoke with.

Compare the request path: buffered synchronous invocation allows 6 megabytes each way, asynchronous invocation allows a 1 megabytes event, and supported streamed responses have a separate limit. If a front door has a smaller limit, store the large object in S three and pass a reference that grants no more access than the recipient needs.

For steady traffic, 200 requests per second times half a second of work gives about 100 concurrent executions. That estimates work in flight, not requests per minute, and is a starting point for capacity planning.

Reserved concurrency carves a share out of the regional account pool and caps that function. Use the cap to protect a database, and the reservation to separate a critical workload from noisy neighbors. Check actual account quotas and observed throttles before assuming the default one thousand concurrent executions are available.

Use reserved concurrency to cap and reserve capacity; it does not pre-initialize code. Provisioned concurrency instead keeps environments ready for a version or alias. It adds cost and handles startup latency, while traffic above the provisioned amount can use on-demand capacity if other limits allow.

SnapStart reduces initialization time by restoring a snapshot for supported configurations. Test that generated identifiers or other state that must be unique are refreshed after restore. SnapStart and provisioned concurrency cannot be used together; neither replaces dependency capacity planning.

In this video, you'll release a Lambda version safely and learn which signals help you diagnose trouble. Publish an immutable version and let production callers use the alias. The example sends ninety percent to version one and ten percent to version two. Move the alias weights without asking callers to change the function name they invoke.

Sam can describe the deployment preference, and CodeDeploy can move traffic. Use deployment hooks and CloudWatch alarms to prove health and roll back when needed. Before the canary, check whether both code versions can safely use the same data schema.

Logs tell you what happened in an individual invocation; find the request ID and never log a secret. Metrics show whether errors, duration or throttles are spreading. Lambda publishes standard service metrics automatically, while the execution role needs permission to write CloudWatch Logs.

Traces can isolate the slow segment. If initialization is quick but one downstream call is slow, look at that dependency before resizing Lambda. Use supported Open Telemetry and tracing configuration, including the required permissions.

In this video, you'll trace Lambda's private database path and design fixed public egress. A V P C attachment gives the function a path to a private database through a managed Hyperplane network interface. The database security group can allow the Lambda security group on T C P port five four three two. A route and security rule do not sign the application in; validate database authentication separately.

For I P version four internet access, traffic takes a different path: a private subnet's default route, a public nat gateway and an internet gateway. Putting Lambda in a public subnet does not give it a public I P. Supported V P C endpoints can avoid that internet path for eligible A W S services.

Trace the partner A P I request from Lambda's network interface to the private subnet default route, then through a public nat gateway and its internet gateway. The external A P I sees the nat gateway's Elastic I P, not an I P owned by the function.

Plan which nat paths can serve the workload during an Availability Zone fault. If there are multiple possible egress paths, the partner must allowlist all of the corresponding public addresses. Include processing and transfer cost in the decision.

In this video, you'll compare Lambda invocation modes and decide who retries work and where to retain failure evidence. A synchronous caller waits within its own timeout. Follow the first request: the Lambda function commits the write, but the response is lost. That leaves the caller unsure whether the business operation completed. A successful transport status alone would not prove the handler succeeded either.

On a retry, use the same idempotency key and return the previously recorded result instead of writing again. Look at the function error or front-door status and correlate logs. Retry only appropriate failures, with bounded backoff and jitter.

An accepted asynchronous invocation only means the Lambda-managed queue took the order event. EventBridge has its own target-delivery policy before acceptance. The order is not written until the function processes the accepted event afterward.

After acceptance, a function error gets two additional attempts by default. Throttling and system errors can be retried within the configured event age, six hours by default. Use the event ID to avoid duplicate writes, and configure where exhausted or expired failures go.

Pick the evidence you need. A Lambda asynchronous destination receives an invocation record with request and response context. A dead-letter queue instead retains the original failed event. Standard S Q S or S N S supports a function dead-letter queue; S three is a destination option for failure records, not a function dead-letter queue.

The failure route itself can fail. Use an execution role allowed to deliver to the destination, check encryption permissions and size limits, then test the expected record arriving. Monitor Destination Delivery Failures so a denied or oversized record does not silently undermine recovery.

With S Q S, Lambda's event source mapping polls a batch. A successful batch can be deleted; by default a failed batch can reappear after the visibility timeout. With partial batch responses configured, successful messages can be removed while failed ones become available for retry.

A stream has a checkpoint and ordered processing within the relevant shard boundaries. A poison record can delay progress; choose retry and age limits where supported. This is neither the separate Lambda asynchronous invocation queue nor a substitute for an idempotent handler and measured throughput.
